podcast.body: An album issued in 1966 featuring original artwork of the Beatles posing with headless baby dolls and raw meat, known as the infamous "butcher cover." This photo, part of a collection by Robert Whitaker, was conceived as a protest against the Vietnam War and possibly a "dig" at EMI for "butchering" the Beatles' UK albums for North American release. A limited number of these albums were sent to stores, causing record store owners to be appalled. Capitol Records, the band's American label, immediately recalled all 60,000 albums distributed and held back another 750,000 in warehouses. A new cover was chosen, depicting the Beatles sitting around a steamer trunk looking annoyed. Many recalled albums simply had the new cover pasted over the old one, which could be carefully steamed off to reveal the original. A sealed copy of the original butcher version in mint condition can be worth $125,000. "In 1966, they issued the Beatles yesterday and today, an album where the original artwork featured the Beatles posing with some headless baby dolls in a bunch of raw meat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
